newsitem.title: IRAQ: Kurdish guerrillas pause before rivals' city.
newsitem.headline: Kurdish guerrillas pause before rivals' city.

text.p: The Patriotic Union of Kurdistan (PUK) began fleeing its last Iraqi stronghold of Sulaimaniya as fighters of its Baghdad-backed rival were poised to move in, a U.N. official said on Monday.

"The PUK has simply left its offices. The theory is they are on their way to the Iranian border. I think it's a matter of hours before something happens," Mogens Hansen, U.N. security officer for the region, told Reuters.

In a statement the PUK said Sulaimaniya was in danger of collapse and appealed to Washington to help it against the rival Kurdistan Democratic Party (KDP), now backed by troops of Iraqi President Saddam Hussein.

"The U.S. administration speaks of southern Iraq, but Saddam's tanks, army and secret police are on the move in the north -- towards Sulaimaniya, which is in imminent danger of collapse," the PUK said in a statement from Ankara.
From the heights of Heibet Sultan mountain, however, there was no sign any Iraqi troops or armour were involved in the latest fighting, an assessment shared by Hansen, the United Nations commander.
Baghdad, which actively backed the KDP assault on the main Kurdish city of Arbil nine days ago, has denied taking part in further operations.
Hundreds of KDP guerrillas, meanwhile, paused to regroup along the Sulaimaniya road. Some slept under trees, as comrades cleaned their rifles or washed in irrigation ditches.
Their commanders said they were awaiting orders to push on toward Sulaimaniya to the southeast, or to turn north to the strategic Dukan dam.
"No decision has been made. The politburo is still discussing what to do," said a senior KDP official who asked not to be identified.

Morale was high among the Kurdish faction, buttressed by anti-personnel carriers, artillery and other heavy weaponry seized from the PUK at Arbil on August 31. Busloads of fighters, some sporting the yellow headband of the KDP, moved into position.
Their war booty included a Soviet-era T-62 tank, seven armoured pesonnel carriers, five Katyusha rocket launchers and truck-mounted heavy machineguns.
"These guys are just waiting for orders to continue on to Sulaimaniya," said Hansen.
Inside the village of Degala and the city of Koi Sanjaq, both further to the west, there were no signs the PUK had made a determined stand when they fell on Sunday.
Instead, the real skirmishes had taken place on earthworks near the main Sulaimaniya road, now littered with spent cartridges.
Thousands of Kurds fled from Degala and Koi Sanjaq in cars, trucks and even bulldozers on Sunday.
Most shops were open in Koi Sanjaq, a city of 80,000, on Monday as scattered residents went about their business cautiously.
The KDP seized the international spotlight on August 31 when, aided by Iraqi President Saddam Hussein, the militia captured Arbil.
The United States retaliated against Saddam by firing 44 cruise missiles on southern Iraq.
